title: Preliminary tests show no lead in water bodies near Iowa detonation, EPA says | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Three days aftervolatile materials were detonatedat an Iowa ammunition plant, a first set of preliminary tests from around the site show no elevated lead levels in public water supplies, the Environmental Protection Agencyannouncedearly Saturday.

“EPA found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake,” the agency wrote in a press release.

“We will continue to provide updates in the coming days as new lab results for over 3,200 air, soil, dust and water samples (collected pre and post detonation) rapidly return and get validated,” it added.

The results come after the US Army detonated nearly five tons of deteriorating lead azide Wednesday at its plant in Middletown, Iowa. The detonation brought concern from residents, elected officials and environmental groups about the material’s potential effects, both on people and the plains of Iowa and neighboring Missouri.

Some of the results started coming into the EPA’s database Friday night after officials spent days collecting samples to try and determine how much lead may have settled in surrounding areas.

“EPA personnel and contractors continue to work around the clock to gather samples, ship those samples to labs, verify results, and transparently communicate those results to the public immediately,” the agency said Friday evening.

Zero airborne lead was detected near the plant about 30 minutes after the explosion and testing performed hours later showed the same result, the EPA said. But experts have cautioned those results need to be followed by additional testing as they only represent one data point.

Air testing conducted by the EPA concluded after 30 hours of zero detection of lead, the agencysaid on X.

Army officials have said a planned detonation was the only safe way to get rid of the dangerous material, which the Army had been aware of since at least March of this year, because it had degraded to the point of being unmovable without potentially triggering an explosive reaction. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives has indicated the materials may have been known to be degraded aboutas far back as 2009.

In the days since the detonation, hundredsof EPA personnel collected over 1,600 air, water, soil and dust samples at more than 180 structures, the agency said ina post on X. Those samples will be compared to the 1,600 collected prior to Wednesday’s explosion.

As of Friday evening, 88% of post-detonation sampling at homes previously sampled was completed, the EPA said.

Environmental groups attempted to stop the detonation with a lawsuit. They were temporarily granted a stay, but a three-judge appeals court panel ultimately ruled to let the explosion move forward. Despite the lawsuit failing to stop the detonation, the environmental groups havevowed to hold the government accountablefor the ensuing clean-up operation.

Before the detonation Wednesday, federal agencies ranging from the EPA to the Federal Emergency Management Agency descended upon the small Iowa town to try to safely evacuate residents and prepare for potential impacts. The residents were given an “all clear” to return to their homes Wednesday night.
